key_findings: Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13, a day after a public proof of concept appeared.

Confluence Data Center 1.x to 9.x is exposed only when the Remote API (XML-RPC and SOAP) is enabled; N-able N-central is exposed where its Legacy API is enabled.
The intruder ran scripted, likely AI-assisted commands, pulled Confluence database credentials, searched for card numbers and reached a cloud data warehouse within about four hours.

recommendations: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first.
If you cannot upgrade, clear the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting in the admin configuration; this may break integrations.
Upgrade N-central to 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) and confirm the Legacy API is disabled.
Investigate exposed systems for signs of compromise using the indicators Rapid7 published.

key_findings: Huntress saw rogue ScreenConnect clients pushed to at least 288 hosts at 48 organisations on November 11 and 205 hosts at 41 organisations in a second wave on November 13.
Operators used the Run Command feature on cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to run commands as SYSTEM; one panel alone reached 190 downstream clients.
Entry appears tied to the third-party RMM+ extension, versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, which accepted a blank access key; ConnectWise disabled five extensions across 400+ partner environments.
SCKit is 16 scripts and config files that install a rogue client, hijack the real client's connection and try to steal technician session cookies using CVE-2026-84869.
Huntress has not seen the jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation succeed in any recovered log.
recommendations: Verify every technician client runs ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later and disable the affected RMM+ extension versions.

Do not connect to a suspected host through ScreenConnect; use WinRM or another out-of-band tool and isolate it until cleaned.
Remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task and the RelayTrap folder, then rotate ScreenConnect credentials and end web sessions from a clean device.

key_findings: Targets were 7 semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing firms, 3 defence or defence-policy bodies and 4 human-rights or civil-society groups, including a Canadian rights body and a US teachers' union.
The cluster ran 25 operations against at least 19 organisations and reached confirmed unauthorised access or data retrieval at 10 of them.
It used a customised fork of the open-source Cairn framework driven by Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 models, plus a custom skill pack not in upstream Cairn.
Entry came from password spraying, brute-forced credentials, unauthenticated cloud-storage writes, login bypasses and open registration endpoints rather than new exploits.
Data taken included over 1 million union member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts and about 150,000 internal documents; Unit 42 assesses China-nexus collection with moderate confidence.
recommendations: Tighten identity hygiene: remove weak, default and shared passwords on internet-facing applications.
Reduce the exposed attack surface, including open registration endpoints and unauthenticated cloud storage.
Patch software affected by older public CVEs.
Monitor for the two IP addresses Unit 42 published for the Cairn hosting and staging servers.

written.plain: The FBI says North Korean hackers stage fake video meetings using real recordings of earlier victims, then trick people into running a so-called fix that infects their computer and empties crypto wallets.

key_findings: Targets are cryptocurrency and Web3 workers, open-source developers and maintainers, and through them their contacts and employers' networks.
Operators take over a victim's messaging account, send contacts a look-alike meeting link and replay the victim's recorded webcam video in a staged session.
Posing as the contact, they claim an audio fault and have the target run an update or paste terminal code, installing a backdoor, keyloggers and a cookie harvester.
More than $400 million was stolen over roughly 18 months and the FBI seized over 900 victim webcam videos; one widely used JavaScript library was nearly compromised.
New elements are AI-generated deepfakes of known crypto figures, attempts on NPM and Rust maintainers, and theft delayed for months after compromise.
recommendations: Join meetings through the official Zoom or Teams app with an invite code rather than a web link.
Keep your camera off until you have verified the inviter, and confirm meetings through a different channel.

written.plain: Hackers are breaking into self-hosted Confluence wiki servers through an old built-in component, then using passwords found there to reach other company systems. Atlassian's cloud version is not affected.

key_findings: Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13, a day after a public proof of concept appeared.
The flaw is unsafe reflection in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x giving unauthenticated remote code execution; CISA scores it 9.8.
Confluence Data Center 1.x to 9.x is exposed only when the Remote API (XML-RPC and SOAP) is enabled; N-able N-central is exposed where its Legacy API is enabled.
The intruder ran scripted, likely AI-assisted commands, pulled Confluence database credentials, searched for card numbers and reached a cloud data warehouse within about four hours.
About twelve hours in, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication.
recommendations: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first.
If you cannot upgrade, clear the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting in the admin configuration; this may break integrations.
Upgrade N-central to 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) and confirm the Legacy API is disabled.
Investigate exposed systems for signs of compromise using the indicators Rapid7 published.

written.action: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing first. If you cannot, switch off Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP). Then check exposed servers for compromise with Rapid7's indicators.
written.exec: One unpatched wiki server gave an intruder a path to a data warehouse and Microsoft 365 within twelve hours; emergency patching is advised.
written.plain: Hackers are breaking into self-hosted Confluence wiki servers through an old built-in component, then using passwords found there to reach other company systems. Atlassian's cloud version is not affected.

key_findings: Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13, a day after a public proof of concept appeared.
The flaw is unsafe reflection in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x giving unauthenticated remote code execution; CISA scores it 9.8.
Confluence Data Center 1.x to 9.x is exposed only when the Remote API (XML-RPC and SOAP) is enabled; N-able N-central is exposed where its Legacy API is enabled.
The intruder ran scripted, likely AI-assisted commands, pulled Confluence database credentials, searched for card numbers and reached a cloud data warehouse within about four hours.
About twelve hours in, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication.
recommendations: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first.
If you cannot upgrade, clear the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting in the admin configuration; this may break integrations.
Upgrade N-central to 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) and confirm the Legacy API is disabled.
Investigate exposed systems for signs of compromise using the indicators Rapid7 published.

written.summary: Rapid7 says its MDR team detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13. The flaw is unauthenticated remote code execution in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x, reachable when Confluence's Remote API is enabled. The intruder harvested database credentials, queried a cloud data warehouse and later signed in to Microsoft 365 as a service account. Confluence 9.2.28 fixes it; Cloud is unaffected.

written.exec: Refrigeration controllers under active attack have six more unfixed flaws; the researchers say only removing internet exposure helps.
written.impact: A joint US fact sheet of November 5 (CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, DoT) warns that actors altering refrigeration controller settings can force continuous heating and defrost cycles, causing inventory loss, fire hazard and loss of temperature visibility.
written.plain: Researchers found six unfixed weaknesses in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers that let outsiders take control without a password. Attack waves on such devices began in October, and Germany's BSI urges keeping them off the internet.

key_findings: Midnight Blue found six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws, stack-based buffer overflows, in Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware up to and including 5.3.2.
A further pre-authentication memory corruption bug sits in the controller's session control component.
CVE numbers are pending and technical details are withheld while coordinated disclosure with Danfoss continues.
Internet scans on November 10 showed hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed, plus over 1,000 Copeland and Dixell and hundreds of Eliwell controllers.
The attack waves began in France on October 11; public exploit code for older AK-SM800A flaws appeared within 48 hours.
recommendations: Inventory which controllers are internet-exposed, including through integrators' 4G modems.
Restrict management interfaces to a VPN, private APN or a highly restrictive firewall IP whitelist.
Do not treat patching or strict session control as sufficient; put effort into reducing exposure.
Treat IP whitelisting as an interim measure only.

written.exec: A supplier's leaked key led to tampered developer tools reaching up to 5,000 users; Cursor has dropped the supplier for inference.
written.plain: Coding-tool maker Cursor says a key it gave supplier Fireworks AI was exposed. Attackers used it to copy data, then posted harmful copies of a popular add-on for about 11 hours on October 29, reaching at most 5,000 users.

key_findings: An attacker used an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks AI, which Fireworks exposed, to copy data from a read-only storage bucket.
The bucket held coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions not in Privacy Mode; under 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed.
Credentials in those traces opened some SaaS tools, archived non-production repositories, limited support data and usage metrics.
On October 29 malicious copies of the Claude Code extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, sat in the marketplace cache for about 11 hours; at most 5,000 users could have received them.
Cursor saw the last attacker activity on November 1 and moved all inference off Fireworks; Fireworks' own bulletin dates its first intrusion to August 3 to October 7.
recommendations: If you installed or updated to Claude Code extension 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 during the window, follow Cursor's October 30 security notice; uninstalling alone may not be enough.
Rotate any exposed keys; admins were sent lists of affected keys.
Fireworks customers: create new API keys, rotate third-party credentials named in your notice and review access logs for those credentials.

written.action: Identify Linux systems running OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on musl libc without PAM that accept password logins, and update to 10.6p2. Until then, disable password authentication or turn SSH off on those systems.
written.exec: The flaw applies only to a narrow combination of settings, but where all four conditions hold the result may be root access.
written.plain: New Zealand's cyber agency warned of a flaw in OpenSSH, the standard tool for logging in to Linux machines remotely, that could let an attacker in as the top-level user on certain lightweight Linux systems.

key_findings: CVE-2026-123158, also called SSHole, is an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on Linux that may allow root access.
All four conditions must hold: version earlier than 10.6p2, musl libc, no Pluggable Authentication Modules, and password logins accepted.
OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes the flaw.
The alert gives no CVSS score and does not say whether the flaw is being exploited.
recommendations: Update to OpenSSH 10.6p2.
As mitigation, disable password authentication or disable SSH.
Identify potentially affected systems in your environment.
Apply vendor patches or mitigations as they become available and follow the OpenSSH release notes.

The first wave targeted Israeli organisations and was destructive in a limited number of cases; a second wave from November 2 reached organisations in several countries with no destruction reported.
Tools included the TSGA backdoor, a TSProxy library, PHP webshells, a network scanner and a wiper that was also run on a VMware ESXi host reached over SSH.
Check Point Research links the tooling to the PhiliKit framework but does not attribute the campaign with confidence and raises a possible false flag.

written.plain: A researcher published an unfixed Windows flaw, named SignDrop, that lets someone who already has basic access to a computer gain full control of it by misusing built-in protections. No fix exists yet.

key_findings: A researcher using the name MSNightmare (Nightmare-Eclipse cluster) published SignDrop on GitHub on November 10, 2026 without coordinated disclosure.

It raises a standard user to SYSTEM without memory corruption, abusing CLFS HMAC authentication and the Defender signature-update RPC interface to plant a file, then sideloading a DLL through consent.exe.
Cyderes reproduced all five stages and got a SYSTEM shell with no UAC prompt; the exploit deletes its planted DLL afterwards.
No CVE or patch exists; Microsoft had not commented as of November 11 and no in-the-wild use was identified as of November 10.
It is the cluster's sixteenth public zero-day in about thirty-one weeks; the researcher's claim that about 80% of installations are vulnerable is unsupported.
recommendations: Inventory the CLFS Authentication Mode registry value across hosts to define which systems to prioritise.
Do not disable CLFS authentication, because that reopens older memory-corruption attack classes.
Restrict untrusted local code execution with application and script control.
Deploy the detections Cyderes lists, such as Defender signature-update RPC calls from outside the Defender service tree and any hid.dll created in the ink directory.
Retain file-creation and image-load telemetry, since the exploit removes its artifact.

written.plain: India's cyber agency published a warning about The Gentlemen, a criminal group that rents out ransomware. It breaks in through remote-access equipment or stolen passwords, copies data, then locks Windows, Linux and virtual servers.

key_findings: The Gentlemen is a financially motivated ransomware-as-a-service group using double extortion; its Go-based payload is obfuscated with Garble and can self-propagate.
It targets Windows, Linux, BSD, NAS devices and VMware ESXi; reported sectors include healthcare, construction, finance and manufacturing.
Initial access is through internet-facing edge devices, RDP and VPN services, or compromised credentials.
Operators spread through Group Policy Objects and the NETLOGON share, disable Microsoft Defender, delete shadow copies and clear event and RDP logs.
Data is exfiltrated with WinSCP before encryption; the advisory lists file hashes, IP addresses and domains but no CVEs.
recommendations: Inventory internet-facing services, disable those not needed and keep management interfaces off the public internet.
Patch firewalls and VPN appliances and enforce MFA for all remote access.
Keep offline, encrypted, immutable backups isolated from production and test restoration.
Review Group Policy Objects, domain admin membership and changes to NETLOGON and SYSVOL regularly.
Do not pay ransoms; report incidents to CERT-In and law enforcement.

recommendations: Deploy GTP-C and GTP-U security and align it with SS7 and Diameter firewalls for cross-protocol visibility.
Treat the IPX interface as untrusted and inspect all traffic more deeply.
Monitor internal signalling protocols and tools, not just the network edge.
Integrate signalling security with IT security and reconsider outsourcing of core networks.

recommendations: Fix basics: default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code or public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and unpatched software.
Assume exposed secrets and misconfigurations will be found quickly and remediate on that basis.
Put AI apps, model gateways and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems.
Watch for misuse through unexpected spend or unusual usage.

Turkish-language comments were found in the rootkit source; the operator is unidentified.
recommendations: Check who can submit jobs to GPU clusters and whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified.

written.action: Take SSH off the internet and require two-factor sign-in for remote access. Patch VMware vCenter and anything still exposed to Log4Shell. Software makers: isolate signing servers and review their logs for unexpected use.
written.exec: Attackers were positioned for a supply-chain attack on a developer's customers; the signing step was blocked, but only just.
written.plain: Kaspersky found that a hacking group spent months inside a Russian software company and tried to tamper with the server that digitally signs its software. Security software blocked that attempt.

key_findings: The victim is a Russia-based developer of industrial software used mainly in Eastern Europe; Kaspersky attributes the intrusion to BO Team (Black Owl) with high confidence.
Entry was through internet-exposed SSH on a Linux terminal server with a password-authenticated service account; Log4Shell in vCenter 7.0.3 then gave root on a hypervisor.
Attackers stayed for several months and reached domain controllers, GitLab, the Ansible server, backups, SIEM and the mail server, stealing its DKIM private key.
Attempts to inject code on the code-signing server were blocked by security software; no signed malware distribution, encryption or destruction is reported.
The stolen DKIM key let them send phishing that passed sender checks, and they mostly lived off the land rather than deploying malware.
recommendations: Remove internet exposure of SSH, disable root SSH login and require two-factor sign-in for VPN, RDP and domain controllers.
Patch vCenter, hypervisors and any software still affected by Log4j.
After an intrusion reset all account passwords, reset krbtgt twice and reissue keys and certificates.
Keep backups on a non-domain server with separate credentials and test restores.
Keep logs at least 30 days and remove plaintext credentials from scripts and directory comments.

Their attempts to inject code on the code-signing server were blocked, and no tampered software release is reported.

written.action: Log and inspect QUIC traffic or block outbound UDP 443 so it falls back to inspectable TCP. Patch Exchange and web servers, review accounts holding the ApplicationImpersonation role and audit Group Policy logon scripts for changes.
written.actor: TGR-STA-0049 (also REF7707, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon)
written.exec: Espionage tools now hide in HTTP/3 traffic that many network monitors skip; unpatched Exchange servers remain the way in.
written.plain: Researchers found a spying group breaking into government networks in Southeast Asia through unpatched email servers and hiding its remote-control traffic inside a newer web protocol many security tools do not inspect.

key_findings: Targets are Southeast Asian government entities; one decoy PDF imitates a Myanmar election commission document, though victim countries are not confirmed.
Entry is through unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers to plant web shells, with phishing using decoy PDFs and DLL sideloading as a second route.
PerfectPioneer, a Go tool with six variants, uses HTTP/3 with HTTP/2 fallback and blocks operators from running noisy or destructive commands.
KUKURAT loads at least 12 modules for keylogging, screenshots, lateral movement and tunnelling, and creates decoy network, registry and file activity.
Activity spans about nine months and included mass mailbox permission changes on Exchange and credential theft from a domain controller.
recommendations: Log and inspect QUIC traffic, or block outbound UDP 443 so HTTP/3 falls back to inspectable TCP.
Audit SYSVOL and Group Policy for unauthorised logon script changes.
Create behavioural rules for rundll32.exe loading comsvcs.dll, including ordinal-based calls.
Review accounts with the ApplicationImpersonation role and watch Exchange logs for repeated Add-MailboxPermission FullAccess grants.

written.summary: Unit 42 describes about nine months of intrusions into Southeast Asian government networks by a group it tracks as TGR-STA-0049. report.doc_id: How AI Agents Become New Targets in GitHub Malware Campaign
key_findings: Researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei identified 22 malicious GitHub links with files designed to make AI-assisted tools execute a concealed payload.
Instruction files describe setup.js as a sealed, signed artifact and tell the assistant not to read it and to run it without confirmation.
A second path uses session-start hooks in project settings such as .claude/settings.json, which can run a command once the developer trusts the repository.
Bitdefender describes setup.js as a multistage loader that can steal source-control, cloud, CI/CD and package-registry credentials, and modify agent configurations for 14 coding tools.
Stolen GitHub or GitLab access can be used to plant malicious files in other repositories and attempt to republish infected packages.
recommendations: Review agent instruction files, startup hooks, MCP definitions and editor tasks before granting an unfamiliar workspace trust.
If execution is suspected, isolate the workstation and revoke exposed tokens from a clean system.

written.title: Kaspersky: Retadup worm's revived servers now deliver CoffeeLoader
written.summary: Kaspersky says servers once used by the Retadup USB worm, disrupted by French police in 2019, now serve a new CoffeeLoader variant. The loader hides in a patched 7-Zip library and uses a packer that runs decryption on the GPU. Kaspersky says its products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems this year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, and it is unclear who runs the servers.
written.plain: An old USB worm that police shut down in 2019 is back and installing a newer malware loader that can bring in further malware. Kaspersky blocked infection attempts on about 15,000 systems.
written.exec: Removable drives can still carry malware that opens the door to later attacks, including from long-dead botnets.
written.action: Block autorun and restrict USB storage on endpoints, scan removable drives, and hunt for a patched 7z.dll running via rundll32.exe from %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%.

key_findings: A new CoffeeLoader variant uses a patched 7z.dll carrying a new version of the Armoury packer, which runs decryption on the GPU via OpenGL instead of OpenCL.
Domains used as Retadup command servers were re-registered about two years ago and first served SmokeLoader, then CoffeeLoader from early 2025.

Kaspersky products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of the year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, far fewer than the 850,000 machines disinfected in 2019.
It is unclear whether the worm's author or another actor revived the servers.

written.plain: Kaspersky described a spying campaign on government networks in Asia and Africa. Hidden access tools take their orders through GitHub, SharePoint and a messaging service, so the traffic looks like normal cloud use.

key_findings: Victims are in Asia and Africa, mainly government; the worked example is two MeshCentral agent instances inside a Taiwanese organisation.

GitDoor receives commands and uploads results through GitHub accounts created between September 2024 and December 2025, and loads plug-ins and shellcode.
GraphDoor authenticates to Microsoft Graph, keeps encrypted victim data in SharePoint and loads plug-ins for keylogging, screenshots and proxy tunnels over Ably.
Kaspersky sees overlaps with Chinese-speaking FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle but says it cannot definitively attribute the activity.
recommendations: Treat the appearance of legitimate remote-management tools in the environment as suspicious.
Do not rely on network detection alone, since command traffic goes to trusted cloud APIs.
Use the indicators Kaspersky publishes in both parts for hunting.

He said France will seek EU sanctions on those responsible, meaning entry bans and asset freezes, as early as possible.
He said further proportionate measures would follow, some of which would not be made public.
He did not name the unit himself and declined to say whether Iran is behind other recent cyberattacks, citing ongoing investigations.

note: CVE, fixed kernels, 2015 origin, timings, CVSS 5.9 match oss-security, CVE record and The Register; exec said almost all Linux servers, overstated (needs multiple RX queues or RPS), reworded

written.action: Update Linux kernels to 6.12.117, 6.18.63, 7.3.4 or your distribution's fixed package, internet-facing servers first. Until then, disable SYN cookies in every network namespace or force a single receive queue with RPS and RFS off.
written.exec: A remote crash flaw in almost all Linux servers; fixes exist and internet-facing systems should be updated first.
written.plain: A flaw called NoisyTCP lets outsiders crash Linux servers over the network without logging in. It has been in Linux since 2015. Fixed versions are out; no attacks are reported.

key_findings: NoisyTCP is a race in the kernel's lockless TCP established-socket lookup that can return a reused, unhashed socket with no listener, causing a NULL dereference and kernel panic.
It is remote and needs no authentication against plain TCP listeners such as Nginx, Apache and SSH in default configurations; in a container the panic takes down the whole host.
The bug dates from a 2015 commit (kernel 4.4) and was fixed upstream on November 3, 2026; stable fixes are 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4.
It needs two or more receive queues or RPS; the researcher reports about 5 seconds to 2 minutes on virtual machines and about 14 hours on a quiet 8-queue bare-metal server.
A second flow can cause a remote use-after-free but is described as hard to trigger; the CVE record's CISA-added score is 5.9 with exploitation marked none.
report.publisher: Hyunwoo Kim (researcher disclosure on oss-security) and the Linux kernel CVE team
recommendations: Apply the kernel fix (commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, shipped in 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4) as the priority.
As a temporary measure, disable SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0) in every network namespace, accepting weaker SYN-flood protection.
Alternatively, serialise to a single receive queue and disable RPS and RFS on interfaces receiving external traffic.

The flaw dates to 2015 and is fixed in kernels 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4. No exploitation is reported.

written.action: Verify WinRAR and other tools on your network are the publisher's signed copies; apply application allowlisting and code-signing checks, and alert on memory that is read, write and execute at once and on PNGs with truncated headers.
written.exec: Trusted programs can be rewritten into malware carriers whose fingerprint changes every run, so hash-based blocking is weak.
written.plain: Security firm ReversingLabs describes BubbleLoader, malware that edits ordinary programs like WinRAR so they secretly load other malware, and changes its fingerprint every time it runs.

key_findings: BubbleLoader patches a program's entry point and adds two PNG images that hold the hidden code; the second PNG is a fake containing encrypted code.
Known hosts include WinRAR, x64dbg, Windows Media Player, the Firefox launcher and virtiofs.
Earliest samples date from February 2026; two activity clusters in mid-September and early October indicate current use.
Runtime polymorphism makes the in-memory payload hash differ on every execution.
ReversingLabs does not say how the tampered programs reach victims (Help Net Security); the final payload varies.
recommendations: Strict application allowlisting and code-signing verification.
Alert on RWX memory and protection changes to ntdll exception routines; flag PNGs with truncated headers.

written.summary: ReversingLabs analysed BubbleLoader, a loader that rewrites a few instructions at a program's entry point and adds two PNG images to turn legitimate software, including WinRAR and Windows Media Player, into a carrier for other malware. It changes its payload's in-memory hash on every run. Samples date from February 2026, with activity clusters in September and October. Delivery method is not stated.

recommendations: Review extensions installed in developer mode that pose as utilities and request permissions such as all URLs, debugger or native messaging.

Look for web-analytics style cookies or storage keys on internal apps where analytics has no reason to appear.
Investigate OAuth activity to OneDrive tenants outside your organisation, especially repeated small JSON writes.

A post on oss-security (Rich Felker, 18 November) advises anyone not needing SCTP to block the module.
recommendations: Block the sctp module where not needed.
Apply kernel updates when released.

note: Compared 16 Nov date, $50 demo, 8/8 backdoored flagged in 16-model test, three backdoor classes, no real-world cases against the CrowdStrike blog

written.action: Scan every open-weight model when it is brought in, before it runs. Flag undisclosed merged fine-tunes, test flagged models for hidden triggers, and decide to block, quarantine or approve on evidence rather than the model card.
written.exec: Downloaded AI models are third-party code; a cheap hidden backdoor is feasible, though so far shown only in the lab.
written.plain: CrowdStrike showed in the lab that freely shared AI models can carry hidden instructions that only switch on with a secret trigger, and described a way to check models before using them.

key_findings: Organisations that download open-weight models they cannot verify are at risk, most of all where agents run tool calls automatically.
A backdoored fine-tune behaves normally until a keyword or date triggers it; a cited demonstration cost about $50 to build.
Three backdoor classes are described: agent, code and safety (refusal removal).
In a lab test of 16 models the pipeline flagged all 8 backdoored ones and recovered a trigger for each.
Fine-tuning can weaken a model's refusals as a side effect even in adapters built for unrelated tasks.
recommendations: Scan every open-weight model statically when it is ingested.
Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery, using the static findings to choose which behaviour to test.
Decide before deployment whether to block, quarantine or approve each model on evidence, not its model card.
Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code.

written.summary: CrowdStrike published lab research on AI models that behave normally until a trigger word or date makes them act maliciously, for example by calling an attacker's address. It cites a demonstration that cost about $50 to build. Its two-stage method, weight comparison then trigger recovery, flagged all eight backdoored models in a 16-model test. No real-world cases are reported.
written.title: CrowdStrike shows how to detect backdoors hidden in open-weight AI model fine-tunes

validation.note: Reviewed against the original CrowdStrike report.

written.action: Tell developers to enter device codes only for sign-ins they started, review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations, and set Copilot CLI cloud session storage and memory to the least permissive setting that works.

written.plain: Microsoft tested how tricking a developer into typing a sign-in code could let a hacker control their AI coding assistant and read their private code. It has not seen this used in real attacks yet.

key_findings: In a controlled simulation, a test account approved a GitHub device-code request started by an attacker-controlled client using the public Copilot CLI client ID.
With that approval researchers could steer a remote-control-enabled Copilot CLI session to run a command, add misleading memory entries, read synced sessions and access private repositories.
The requested scopes included repo, read:user, read:org, gist and codespace, chosen by the client that starts the flow.
The technique applies to any public client supporting the device flow; Microsoft has not observed these four outcomes in the wild.
Microsoft cites earlier device-code phishing campaigns including Storm-2372 and EvilTokens, which it helped disrupt in September 2026.
recommendations: Approve device codes only for sign-ins you started yourself, even on the genuine github.com page.
Review GitHub Copilot CLI session storage and remote-control policy and choose the least permissive setting.
Review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations and limit repository access by role.
Review Copilot Memory for suspicious entries, and connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps for visibility.

written.summary: Microsoft researchers showed in a lab that a phished GitHub device-code approval for the Copilot CLI client could let an attacker steer a remotely controllable agent session, plant misleading memory entries, read cloud-synced sessions and reach private repositories. These are proof-of-concept results, not attacks seen in the wild. Microsoft added two Defender XDR detections for the email and Teams lures.
written.title: Microsoft: one phished device-code approval could let attackers steer AI coding agents

key_findings: Between October 3 and November 5 Amazon saw two campaigns it assesses, with moderate confidence, used ARTEX agents run by disparate Chinese-nexus groups.
Campaign 1 found exposed AI gateways and builders (One API, LiteLLM, Dify, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI and others), extracted upstream provider keys, validated and pooled them.
Stolen keys funded the model gateway driving further key hunting; agents also used CVE-2025-3248, CVE-2026-28797, a One API header bypass and the LiteLLM default master key.
Campaign 2 attacked identity verification at two crypto exchanges with real-time deepfake video and forged ID photos; the vendor rejected every recorded attempt.
Amazon did not watch the activity live and could not verify the agents' reported outcomes; it publishes 11 IP indicators.
recommendations: Fix basics: default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code or public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and unpatched software.
Assume exposed secrets and misconfigurations will be found quickly and remediate on that basis.
Put AI apps, model gateways and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems.
Watch for misuse through unexpected spend or unusual usage.

written.action: Find every Java runtime, including ones bundled in third-party apps, containers and appliances. Apply Oracle and vendor patches, internet-facing systems first. Until patched, validate and size-limit Base64 input and restrict unauthenticated access. Siemens Industrial Edge Management users: block direct internet access to IEM Pro and Virtual until Siemens releases a fix.
written.exec: Java is embedded across business applications, appliances and containers; this flaw allows takeover without credentials, so patching needs an inventory first.
written.plain: The US cyber agency says a serious flaw in Java, software built into a huge number of business systems, must be patched right away. Specially crafted data could let an outsider take over a system without logging in.
products: Siemens Industrial Edge Management Pro V1/V2 and Virtual

key_findings: CVE-2026-114938 ('Java4Shell') is a critical memory-corruption flaw in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM, part of the JDK.
Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow unauthenticated remote code execution.
Java runtimes are often bundled inside third-party applications, container images and appliances and may not appear as separate inventory entries.
The CISA alert does not state that exploitation has been observed.

SecurityWeek (19 Nov): GreyNoise saw over 150 requests matching a Java4Shell attack from five IP addresses and no successful intrusions on its sensors; Previdian logged nine attempts from six IPs on 18 and 19 November; Cisco knows of proof-of-concept code but no malicious use.
report.publisher: CISA, with the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security contributing
recommendations: Identify affected Java installations, including bundled runtimes in applications, containers and appliances.
Apply Java and vendor patches as soon as available, prioritising internet-facing systems.
If patching must wait, restrict and validate Base64 input at the application boundary, enforce input-size limits and limit unauthenticated access.
Review Oracle's November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update for affected products and versions.
Monitor for rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes and suspicious Java processes.

written.summary: CISA urged immediate patching of CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell), a critical memory-corruption flaw in the x86-64 HotSpot JVM's Base64 decoder that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution. SecurityWeek reports on 19 November that GreyNoise saw over 150 matching requests from five IP addresses, without successful intrusions on its sensors. Cisco, Siemens, Elastic and Red Hat have issued advisories; Cisco has no fixes yet.
written.title: CISA: patch critical Java flaw 'Java4Shell' (CVE-2026-114938) immediately

validation.note: CVE-2026-114938 was not found in NVD at the last check.

written.action: Verify WinRAR and other tools on your network are the publisher's signed copies; apply application allowlisting and code-signing checks, and alert on memory that is read, write and execute at once and on PNGs with truncated headers.
written.exec: Trusted programs can be rewritten into malware carriers whose fingerprint changes every run, so hash-based blocking is weak.
written.plain: Security firm ReversingLabs describes BubbleLoader, malware that edits ordinary programs like WinRAR so they secretly load other malware, and changes its fingerprint every time it runs.

key_findings: BubbleLoader patches the entry point of a benign program and appends two PNG files; the host then decrypts and reflectively loads a final payload in memory.
Hosts seen include WinRAR, x64dbg, Windows Media Player, a Firefox launcher and virtiofs; the post names no victims or sectors and the final payload varies by sample.
Earliest samples date from February 2026, with two activity clusters in mid-September and early October.

It overwrites padding bytes in the payload with timestamp-derived randomness on each run, so the in-memory hash changes every execution, and hooks RtlPcToFileHeader in ntdll so the payload can handle exceptions.
The second PNG is a fake with a truncated header, which ReversingLabs offers as a static detection signal; the post does not say how the altered programs reach victims.
recommendations: Enforce strict application allowlisting and code-signing verification, especially for common utilities such as WinRAR.
Have EDR alert on read-write-execute memory allocated with VirtualAlloc and on protection changes to the ntdll routine RtlPcToFileHeader.
Add static rules for embedded PNGs with a truncated header.
Rely on behavioural memory analysis and entry-point integrity checks, not only static payload hashes.

written.actor: REF3364 (Elastic's tracking name; financially motivated, unattributed)
written.summary: Elastic Security Labs describes REF3364, a Linux cryptomining operation seen in late October 2026. Access came through an exposed Ray job agent. The toolkit, SANSAR, adds a kernel rootkit, a modified NVIDIA NVML wrapper that reports 0% GPU use and random temperatures, and an Ethereum-assisted backdoor. written.exec: Hijacked AI compute raises costs and takes capacity from real workloads, and fake monitoring readings hide it.
written.action: Do not expose Ray job APIs to the internet, restrict who can submit jobs, and check hosts for a modified NVML library, unknown DKMS modules such as acpi_thermal_mgr and initramfs changes.

key_findings: Organisations running Linux GPU hosts for AI or ML work are the target; three hosts were hit in an intrusion tracked as REF3364 between 22 and 25 October 2026.
Initial access was an internet-reachable Ray job agent that accepted job submissions without authentication, followed by a reverse shell and an added SSH key.
The Rust orchestrator SANSAR takes commands over Tor, runs XMRig and SRBMiner-MULTI for mining, and can open shells and run a TCP SYN flood task.
A kernel rootkit (acpi_thermal_mgr.ko) hides selected processes, files and sockets, and a modified NVML library reports 0% GPU use with random temperature and power readings.
A separate netns backdoor gets its controller address from an Ethereum contract through public RPC and opens a shell on port 8080.
recommendations: Check who can submit jobs to GPU clusters and do not leave job agents such as Ray reachable without authentication.
Check whether GPU monitoring libraries such as NVML have been modified.

Zero-day exploits averaged 8 a month in 2025 and 11 in 2026, with a spike to 22 in August 2026.
LLMJacking cases handled by Mandiant saw single-day fraudulent charges above $100,000 and cumulative abuse reaching $1 million before remediation; one route was LiteLLM flaw CVE-2026-40217.
recommendations: Use Mandiant's published hardening guide and defence framework for machine-speed, LLM-enabled offensive tooling.

Verify LLM-generated proof-of-concept exploits before acting on them; many published ones do not work.

sources.name: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere

written.action: Apply the Broadcom patch for CVE-2026-123890 to vCenter Server now, restrict inbound access and egress from vCenter, and hunt with the GTIG indicators and the Mandiant VCSA hardening tool.

attribution.claim: Suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221)

written.exec: A suspected state-backed group used an unpatched vCenter flaw to control virtualisation hosts, which hold most servers in a company; the fix is available now.
written.plain: Google says a suspected China-linked spy group exploited a previously unknown flaw in VMware vCenter to take control of virtual server infrastructure. A patch is out.

key_findings: CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter Server is an unauthenticated SRP-6a session key disclosure over DCE/RPC leading to authentication bypass as administrator@vsphere.local; Broadcom patch page linked from the post.
The campaign used two zero-days in total; the other is the BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw CVE-2026-102764 from GTIG's 15 October post.
The actor moved from a BeyondTrust appliance to internal Linux appliances without EDR, then to vCenter and ESXi.
Five newly identified malware families and utilities are described, including the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, BONESAW and SAWSNAKE; LAZYBONES was also deployed.
The post names no victim organisations or countries.
recommendations: Apply the Broadcom patch immediately.
Use the Mandiant VCSA Hardening and Logging Tool after testing and change control.
Hunt with the YARA rules and indicators in the GTI collection.

sources.name: Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere

written.summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group says ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor it formerly tracked as UNC5221, exploited CVE-2026-123890 in VMware vCenter Server, an unauthenticated authentication bypass disclosed on 19 November. GTIG reports the campaign used two zero-days and new malware, moving from a BeyondTrust appliance to vCenter and ESXi. No victims are named.
written.title: Google: ARMORY CASTLE exploits vCenter zero-day CVE-2026-123890 in espionage campaign

validation.note: Original GTIG post read in full; investigating firm is the primary source.

note: Date 16 Nov, 22 zero-days in August vs 8 per month in 2025, LLMJacking over 100,000 USD in a day, first automated exploit agent, LiteLLM CVE checked against GTIG post

written.title: Google threat intelligence: attackers move to autonomous multi-agent intrusion frameworks
written.summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant report threat actors are using open-source agentic pentesting tools in live intrusions and say they found a fully automated exploitation agent for the first time. The report also describes LLM credential theft resold for profit and AI coding-assistant configuration abuse, and says zero-day exploits rose to 22 in August.
written.plain: Google says criminals and state groups now use AI agents that run attacks largely on their own, and that stolen AI account credentials are being resold.
written.exec: Faster exploit development shortens patch windows and puts AI API keys and developer tooling in attackers' sights.
written.action: Shorten patch cycles for internet-facing systems, rotate and monitor LLM API keys, and audit AI tool config files such as .claude/settings.json in repositories.
written.impact: Report-level findings; named cases include PaperCut and LiteLLM flaws and LLMJacking charges above $100,000 in a day.

key_findings: Open-source agentic pentesting tools used in live intrusions
First fully automated vulnerability exploitation agent found
Zero-day exploits at 22 in August 2026 versus 8 per month average in 2025
LLMJacking: single-day fraudulent charges above $100,000
recommendations: Shorten patch cycles
Rotate and monitor LLM API keys
Audit AI tool configs in repositories

validation.note: Primary source: the vendor's own report, read in full.

note: Compared CVEs, versions, public PoC for CVE-2026-123007, no in-the-wild statement, HTTP/2 workaround and F5 bulletins against CERT-FR, Rapid7 and KrCERT/CC

written.action: Check every NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus server that serves HTTP/2. Apply the fixed versions from F5 bulletins K000163926 and K000163928, or disable HTTP/2 until patched (remove http2 from the listen line, or set http2 off on 1.25.0 and earlier). Review exposed servers for signs of compromise.
written.exec: NGINX is among the most widely used web servers and proxies; an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw with a public proof of concept makes exposed servers urgent to patch or mitigate.
written.plain: French cyber agency warns of two flaws in the NGINX web server that could let an attacker run code on a server over HTTP/2, with public attack code available for one of them.

key_findings: Two flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2.
Affected: NGINX Open Source 1.31.x before 1.31.9 and versions before 1.30.7; NGINX Plus 3.1.x-3.2.x before 3.7.3.0.1 and 3.7.x before 37.0.8.1.
CERT-FR knows of a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007; in-the-wild exploitation is not stated.

KrCERT/CC lists five NGINX Plus and Open Source flaws fixed by F5: CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow) and use-after-free CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-113425; it urges updating to the fixed versions (Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9).
recommendations: Disable HTTP/2 as an interim workaround.

written.summary: CERT-FR warns that two flaws in F5 NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2. It knows of a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007. Affected are Open Source 1.31.x before 1.31.9 and earlier branches before 1.30.7, and Plus before the fixed releases. Disabling HTTP/2 is an interim workaround. KrCERT/CC lists three further use-after-free flaws fixed in the same F5 update.
written.title: CERT-FR: NGINX flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2; public PoC exists

validation.note: Compared CERT-FR (primary) with Rapid7 (PoC author): CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 flaw, fixes 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, public PoC, no in-the-wild exploitation stated. Rapid7 notes its PoC needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 data and a specific x86-64 glibc, and gives no HTTP/2-off workaround; that workaround is CERT-FR advice. Not compared: CVE-2026-123633 (only CERT-FR).

written.title: F5 warns of six critical BIG-IP flaws in the TMM data plane; hotfixes only
written.summary: F5 disclosed six critical stack-based buffer overflows in the BIG-IP Traffic Management Microkernel, CVSS 9.8, that can crash the data plane before authentication on specific virtual-server setups, including iRules and one APM policy. The report says they may allow remote code execution. F5 lists no exploitation. Fixes are engineering hotfixes only, with no workaround.
written.plain: F5 reported six serious flaws in its BIG-IP load balancers that an attacker with no login could use to crash the device, and possibly run code, on certain configurations.
written.exec: BIG-IP sits at the network edge of many large organisations; hotfix-only fixes mean teams must request builds rather than apply a routine update.
written.action: Check whether BIG-IP virtual servers use the affected iRules or the APM policy named in F5 bulletin K000164058, request the engineering hotfixes, and restrict exposure of data-plane listeners until patched.

key_findings: Six stack-based buffer overflows in the TMM data plane, CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) and 9.3 (v4.0).
Four reported by watchTowr, two found by F5; no exploitation listed in the advisories.
Engineering hotfixes only; no workaround.
recommendations: Request F5 hotfixes (K000164058, K4918).

validation.note: Search shows F5 advisories (K000163939, K000163937) and SecurityOnline reporting a different count (seven advisories, APM RCE CVE-2026-123637 at 9.8); F5 portal pages would not render, so the six-critical count and CVSS rest on The Hacker News. Recheck against F5 K000164058.

written.plain: Microsoft fixed three flaws in SharePoint and OneNote that could let an attacker run their own code on a computer or server. No attacks are known.

Run software as a non-administrative user and apply least privilege.
Segment the network and place internet-facing services in a DMZ.

written.action: Government defenders: learn how SoftEther VPN normally behaves on your network and hunt for unexpected SoftEther services; use the IOC list and YARA rules Rapid7 published, and TLS inspection where available.

attribution.note: Rapid7 attributes the tool to Webworm, a China-aligned APT, with moderate confidence

written.date_note: Date of Rapid7's publication; activity dates are not stated in the post
written.exec: A China-aligned espionage group is using a rebuilt VPN tool that avoids malware detection, aimed at government networks.
written.plain: Security firm Rapid7 says a China-aligned spying group called Webworm uses a modified copy of the legitimate SoftEther VPN program to reach government networks without classic malware.

key_findings: Rapid7 describes a custom build of SoftEther VPN Bridge (based on version 4.44, build 9807) rebuilt from source, with renamed branding, changed HTTP endpoints and handshake so stock clients cannot connect.
The resource archive is embedded in the binary and the configuration is stored encrypted with a custom cipher.
Rapid7 attributes the tool to Webworm with moderate confidence, citing TTPs matching ESET's earlier reporting and hosting infrastructure linked to the group before.
Webworm is described as a China-aligned APT focused on governmental organizations, especially in Europe; the post gives no victim counts or country list.
recommendations: Learn SoftEther's normal behaviour on the network, since the actor can easily change endpoints and watermark.
Use Rapid7's published IOC list and YARA rules; detect via TLS inspection where available.

written.summary: Rapid7 published research on a modified build of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge that it attributes, with moderate confidence, to Webworm, a China-aligned group known for targeting governments, especially in Europe. The build changes branding, endpoints and handshake and encrypts its configuration to evade detection. Rapid7 names no victims.
written.title: Rapid7: Webworm uses custom SoftEther VPN bridge to spy on governments without malware

validation.note: Single vendor research post by Rapid7, read in full; attribution is Rapid7's own at moderate confidence.

written.action: Check every NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus server that serves HTTP/2. Apply the fixed versions from F5 bulletins K000163926 and K000163928, or disable HTTP/2 until patched (this covers only the HTTP/2 flaws; the resolver, HTTP/3 and mail proxy flaws need the fixed versions, 1.30.7 or 1.31.9) (remove http2 from the listen line, or set http2 off on 1.25.0 and earlier). Affected: NGINX Open Source 1.31.x before 1.31.9 and versions before 1.30.7; NGINX Plus 3.1.x-3.2.x before 3.7.3.0.1 and 3.7.x before 37.0.8.1.
CERT-FR knows of a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007; in-the-wild exploitation is not stated.

KrCERT/CC lists five NGINX Plus and Open Source flaws fixed by F5: CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow) and use-after-free CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-113425; it urges updating to the fixed versions (Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9). nginx.org titles them: CVE-2026-123007 memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control (major); CVE-2026-123633 use-after-free in HTTP/2 (medium); CVE-2026-123634 use-after-free in the resolver (medium); CVE-2026-121810 use-after-free in HTTP/3 (medium); CVE-2026-113425 use-after-free in the mail proxy module (major).
recommendations: Disable HTTP/2 as an interim workaround for the HTTP/2 flaws only; it does not mitigate the resolver, HTTP/3 or mail proxy flaws.

note: Compared 288/48 and 205/41 hosts, dates, RMM+ 1.0.31/1.0.32, 26.6.5, no technician jump observed against Huntress and BleepingComputer; 400+ partner environments was about 400 in sources, now about 400

written.action: Confirm technician clients run ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later, disable RMM+ extension 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, review Run Command history, and check endpoints for a second ScreenConnect client. Do not connect to suspect hosts through ScreenConnect.
written.exec: Hundreds of managed endpoints were hit through a faulty third-party add-on; the feared spread to IT providers' own machines has not been observed.
written.plain: Attackers pushed fake copies of ConnectWise ScreenConnect remote-support software to hundreds of computers. Their toolkit tries to steal the login session cookie of any IT technician who connects to an infected machine, but researchers have not seen that step work.

key_findings: Huntress saw rogue ScreenConnect clients pushed to at least 288 hosts at 48 organisations on November 11 and 205 hosts at 41 organisations in a second wave on November 13.
Operators used the Run Command feature on cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to run commands as SYSTEM; one panel alone reached 190 downstream clients.
Entry appears tied to the third-party RMM+ extension, versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, which accepted a blank access key; ConnectWise disabled five extensions across 400+ partner environments.

SCKit is 16 scripts and config files that install a rogue client, hijack the real client's connection and try to steal the technician's .aspxauth session cookie (and browser cookie stores) to replay against the panel. Huntress describes CVE-2026-84869 (client flaw before 26.6.5) as background, not as the method SCKit uses.
Huntress has not seen the jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation succeed in any recovered log.
recommendations: Verify every technician client runs ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later and disable the affected RMM+ extension versions.
Review Run Command and Toolbox history for unexpected mass activity and check endpoints for a second, unauthorised ScreenConnect client.
Do not connect to a suspected host through ScreenConnect; use WinRM or another out-of-band tool and isolate it until cleaned.
Remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task and the RelayTrap folder, then rotate ScreenConnect credentials and end web sessions from a clean device.

written.summary: Huntress reports two waves of attacks, on November 11 and 13, using ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to install rogue clients on 288 and then 205 hosts, apparently via a flawed third-party RMM+ extension. The SCKit toolkit tries to steal a technician's session cookie and replay it against the panel; Huntress has not seen that succeed. It names CVE-2026-84869 (fixed in 26.6.5) only as background, not as SCKit's method.
written.title: Huntress: rogue ScreenConnect clients pushed to hundreds of hosts in SCKit attacks; ConnectWise disables extensions

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Huntress report. ConnectWise's advisories page was then read in full: its newest entry is the Cloud Backup notice updated November 4, with no November notice on the ScreenConnect attacks; the separate security bulletins list did not render.

note: CVE, 2015 origin, timings, workarounds, RX-queue requirement match oss-security and The Register; fixed kernels, CISA-ADP 5.9 and exploitation none match the CVE record; 5.15.225 lacks fix per seclists; summary trimmed from 78 to 73 words

written.action: Update Linux kernels to 6.12.117, 6.18.63, 7.3.4 or your distribution's fixed package, internet-facing servers first. Until then, disable SYN cookies in every network namespace or force a single receive queue with RPS and RFS off.
written.exec: A remote crash flaw in Linux servers (kernels since 2015) that use multiple receive queues or RPS; fixes exist and internet-facing systems should be updated first.
written.plain: A flaw called NoisyTCP lets outsiders crash Linux servers over the network without logging in. It has been in Linux since 2015. Fixed versions are out; no attacks are reported.

key_findings: NoisyTCP is a race in the kernel's lockless TCP established-socket lookup that can return a reused, unhashed socket with no listener, causing a NULL dereference and kernel panic.
It is remote and needs no authentication against plain TCP listeners such as Nginx, Apache and SSH in default configurations; in a container the panic takes down the whole host.
The bug dates from a 2015 commit (kernel 4.4) and was fixed upstream on November 3, 2026; stable fixes are 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4.
It needs two or more receive queues or RPS; the researcher reports about 5 seconds to 2 minutes on virtual machines and about 14 hours on a quiet 8-queue bare-metal server.
A second flow can cause a remote use-after-free but is described as hard to trigger; the CVE record's CISA-added score is 5.9 with exploitation marked none.
report.publisher: Hyunwoo Kim (researcher disclosure on oss-security) and the Linux kernel CVE team
recommendations: Apply the kernel fix (commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, shipped in 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4) as the priority.
As a temporary measure, disable SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0) in every network namespace, accepting weaker SYN-flood protection.
Alternatively, serialise to a single receive queue and disable RPS and RFS on interfaces receiving external traffic.

written.summary: Researcher Hyunwoo Kim disclosed NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) on November 16 after a distribution embargo ended. A race in the Linux kernel's TCP socket lookup lets a remote, unauthenticated sender panic servers running ordinary TCP services; in containers the whole host goes down. The flaw dates to 2015 and is fixed in kernels 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4. No exploitation is reported. A 19 November oss-security post says the 5.15 LTS release 5.15.225 lacks the fix and shares an unofficial backport.

written.date_note: Date of OpenSourceMalware's published research; the repositories were created in waves from October 22.
written.exec: Stolen server secrets from Next.js sites are being committed to public GitHub repositories, so anyone can read them; unpatched sites are exposed.

key_findings: OpenSourceMalware named the campaign React2STEAL and identified 45 repositories across 44 GitHub accounts running a scan.yml GitHub Actions workflow.

The pipeline tries React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182), the CVE-2025-29927 middleware bypass and an SSRF through /_next/image to cloud instance metadata, then collects environment variables, credentials and config files.
At least 1,281 unique victim hostnames across about 1,100 domains were found; results were still being committed about every 11 minutes on November 17.
OpenSourceMalware lists the threat actor as unknown and says it does not know whether the same operator ran the earlier wfx-loot campaign.
recommendations: Upgrade React and Next.js to fixed versions.
Strip or reject x-middleware-subrequest at the proxy or WAF until upgraded.
Rotate every secret the server could reach and enforce IMDSv2.

written.title: Kaspersky: Retadup worm's revived servers now deliver CoffeeLoader
written.summary: Kaspersky says servers once used by the Retadup USB worm, disrupted by French police in 2019, now serve a new CoffeeLoader variant. The loader hides in a patched 7-Zip library and uses a packer that runs decryption on the GPU. Kaspersky says its products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems this year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, and it is unclear who runs the servers.
written.plain: An old USB worm that police shut down in 2019 is back and installing a newer malware loader that can bring in further malware. Kaspersky blocked infection attempts on about 15,000 systems.
written.exec: Removable drives can still carry malware that opens the door to later attacks, including from long-dead botnets.
written.action: Block autorun and restrict USB storage on endpoints, scan removable drives, and hunt for a patched 7z.dll running via rundll32.exe from %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%.

key_findings: A new CoffeeLoader variant uses a patched 7z.dll carrying a new version of the Armoury packer, which runs decryption on the GPU via OpenGL instead of OpenCL.
Domains used as Retadup command servers were re-registered about two years ago and first served SmokeLoader, then CoffeeLoader from early 2025.

Kaspersky products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of the year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, far fewer than the 850,000 machines disinfected in 2019.
It is unclear whether the worm's author or another actor revived the servers.

written.action: Treat any unapproved remote-management tool such as a MeshCentral agent as suspicious, review servers for unexpected GitHub, Microsoft Graph, SharePoint or Ably traffic, and load Kaspersky's published indicators into detection.
written.exec: Espionage tools are hiding inside traffic to trusted cloud services, making them harder to spot with normal network filtering.
written.org: Government bodies in Asia and Africa
written.plain: Kaspersky described a spying campaign on government networks in Asia and Africa. Hidden access tools take their orders through GitHub, SharePoint and a messaging service, so the traffic looks like normal cloud use.

key_findings: Victims are in Asia and Africa, mainly government; the worked example is two MeshCentral agent instances inside a Taiwanese organisation.
The entry point is unknown; evidence suggests reuse of an earlier infection, after which the MeshCentral agent was used for DLL sideloading and payload drops.
GitDoor receives commands and uploads results through GitHub accounts created between September 2024 and December 2025, and loads plug-ins and shellcode.
GraphDoor authenticates to Microsoft Graph, keeps encrypted victim data in SharePoint and loads plug-ins for keylogging, screenshots and proxy tunnels over Ably.
Kaspersky sees overlaps with Chinese-speaking FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle but says it cannot definitively attribute the activity.
recommendations: Treat the appearance of legitimate remote-management tools in the environment as suspicious.
Do not rely on network detection alone, since command traffic goes to trusted cloud APIs.
Use the indicators Kaspersky publishes in both parts for hunting.

written.summary: Kaspersky's two-part report describes Operation ShadowCloud, found in early 2026, against mainly government networks in Asia and Africa. Attackers abused a MeshCentral agent to sideload loaders that run GitDoor, which takes commands through GitHub, and GraphDoor, which uses Microsoft Graph and SharePoint. Plug-ins add keylogging, screenshots and proxies over the Ably messaging service. Kaspersky notes overlaps with Chinese-speaking groups but makes no firm attribution.

written.plain: Hackers are breaking into self-hosted Confluence wiki servers through an old built-in component, then using passwords found there to reach other company systems. Atlassian's cloud version is not affected.

key_findings: Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13; a public proof of concept targeting N-able N-central had been published on November 12.
The flaw is unsafe reflection in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x giving unauthenticated remote code execution; CISA scores it 9.8.
Confluence Data Center 1.x to 9.x is exposed only when the Remote API (XML-RPC and SOAP) is enabled; N-able N-central is exposed where its Legacy API is enabled.
The intruder ran scripted, likely AI-assisted commands, pulled Confluence database credentials, searched for card numbers and reached a cloud data warehouse within about four hours.
About twelve hours in, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication.
recommendations: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first.
If you cannot upgrade, clear the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting in the admin configuration; this may break integrations.
Upgrade N-central to 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) and confirm the Legacy API is disabled.
Investigate exposed systems for signs of compromise using the indicators Rapid7 published.

written.action: Update Linux kernels to 6.12.117, 6.18.63, 7.3.4 or your distribution's fixed package, internet-facing servers first. Until then, disable SYN cookies in every network namespace or force a single receive queue with RPS and RFS off.
written.exec: A remote crash flaw in Linux servers (kernels since 2015) that use multiple receive queues or RPS; fixes exist and internet-facing systems should be updated first.
written.plain: A flaw called NoisyTCP lets outsiders crash Linux servers over the network without logging in. It has been in Linux since 2015. Fixed versions are out; no attacks are reported.

key_findings: NoisyTCP is a race in the kernel's lockless TCP established-socket lookup that can return a reused, unhashed socket with no listener, causing a NULL dereference and kernel panic.
It is remote and needs no authentication against plain TCP listeners such as Nginx, Apache and SSH in default configurations; in a container the panic takes down the whole host.
The bug dates from a 2015 commit (kernel 4.4) and was fixed upstream on November 3, 2026; stable fixes are 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4.
It needs two or more receive queues or RPS; the researcher reports about 5 seconds to 2 minutes on virtual machines and about 14 hours on a quiet 8-queue bare-metal server.
A second flow can cause a remote use-after-free but is described as hard to trigger; the CVE record's CISA-added score is 5.9 with exploitation marked none.
report.publisher: Hyunwoo Kim (researcher disclosure on oss-security) and the Linux kernel CVE team
recommendations: Apply the kernel fix (commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, shipped in 6.12.117, 6.18.63 and 7.3.4) as the priority.
As a temporary measure, disable SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0) in every network namespace, accepting weaker SYN-flood protection.
Alternatively, serialise to a single receive queue and disable RPS and RFS on interfaces receiving external traffic.

written.action: Check every NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus server that serves HTTP/2. Apply the fixed versions from F5 bulletins K000163926 and K000163928, or disable HTTP/2 until patched (this covers only the HTTP/2 flaws; the resolver, HTTP/3 and mail proxy flaws need the fixed versions, 1.30.7 or 1.31.9) (remove http2 from the listen line, or set http2 off on 1.25.0 and earlier). Review exposed servers for signs of compromise.
written.exec: NGINX is among the most widely used web servers and proxies; an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw with a public proof of concept makes exposed servers urgent to patch or mitigate.
written.plain: French cyber agency warns of two flaws in the NGINX web server that could let an attacker run code on a server over HTTP/2, with public attack code available for one of them.

key_findings: Two flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2.
Affected: NGINX Open Source 1.31.x before 1.31.9 and versions before 1.30.7; NGINX Plus 3.1.x-3.2.x before 3.7.3.0.1 and 3.7.x before 37.0.8.1.
CERT-FR knows of a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007; in-the-wild exploitation is not stated.

KrCERT/CC lists five NGINX Plus and Open Source flaws fixed by F5: CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow) and use-after-free CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-113425; it urges updating to the fixed versions (Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9). nginx.org titles them: CVE-2026-123007 memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control (major); CVE-2026-123633 use-after-free in HTTP/2 (medium); CVE-2026-123634 use-after-free in the resolver (medium); CVE-2026-121810 use-after-free in HTTP/3 (medium); CVE-2026-113425 use-after-free in the mail proxy module (major).
recommendations: Disable HTTP/2 as an interim workaround for the HTTP/2 flaws only; it does not mitigate the resolver, HTTP/3 or mail proxy flaws.

written.summary: CERT-FR warns that two flaws in F5 NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2; a public proof of concept exists for CVE-2026-123007. Open Source before 1.31.9 (1.30.7 on the older branch) and Plus before the fixed releases are affected. Disabling HTTP/2 is an interim workaround for those two only. Per nginx.org, three more flaws fixed in the same update (resolver, HTTP/3, mail proxy) are not covered.

Confirm the Legacy API is disabled; HF3 removes it.
Upgrade all Agents and Probes following N-able's guidance.

Review N-central servers and managed systems for signs of compromise.

written.action: Inventory every Java runtime, including bundled ones, and install the fixed releases (for example 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1), internet-facing systems first. See Rapid7's advisory for compensating controls where patching is not possible.
written.exec: A serious flaw in widely used Java versions, with a CISA alert urging immediate patching; fixes are available.
written.plain: Security firm Rapid7 and the US cyber agency warned of a serious flaw in recent versions of Java that could let outsiders run their own code. Oracle has released fixes.

key_findings: Memory corruption in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM; specially crafted input could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (CISA).
OpenJDK lists releases 17, 21, 25 and 27 as affected; Oracle fixed versions include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1.

Rapid7 gives Oracle's CVSS v3.1 score as 8.1 (High); neither Rapid7 nor CISA reports exploitation in the wild. SecurityWeek (Nov 19) reports attempts: GreyNoise saw over 150 requests from five IP addresses and no successful intrusions on its sensors; Previdian logged nine attempts from six IPs and says its data cannot confirm compromise.
Researchers at Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against several Java applications; Rapid7 says a reliable exploit needs significant extra work.
recommendations: Apply Oracle's November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update or the OpenJDK fixed releases, internet-facing systems first.
Inventory all JDKs and Java runtimes, including bundled ones; use compensating controls such as Base64 input validation where patching is not possible.

written.plain: Researchers disclosed 14 weaknesses in Copeland XWEB EVO devices that control commercial refrigeration. The maker no longer updates these devices, and attackers began probing two of the flaws within a day.

key_findings: VulnCheck disclosed 14 flaws, CVE-2026-124002 through CVE-2026-124015, in Dixell/Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors including the 300D, 500D and 500 EVO.
They allow unauthenticated root command execution via the login page and a console script, and include a hardcoded administrator password and a daily password derivable from MAC address and date.
The EVO family is end of software support with no fixes after March 16, 2026; current firmware 5.8.8 is affected by several findings.
Internet scans show roughly 1,660 to 1,960 exposed EVO hosts.
Exploitation was seen for two flaws: config writes (CVE-2026-124014) from November 12 22:00 UTC and root execution probes (CVE-2026-124010) from November 13.
recommendations: Keep XWEB EVO devices off the public internet and segment them behind a VPN.
Plan migration to a supported platform, because firmware 5.8.8 will not be patched.
Hunt for the request patterns and source addresses VulnCheck published.

written.exec: Ransomware on industrial firms keeps rising and manufacturing bears most of it; remote access and edge devices are the common entry.
written.plain: Security firm Dragos counted 1,266 ransomware attacks on factories and other industrial companies in three months, 11% more than the previous quarter. Most began through remote-access equipment or stolen VPN passwords.

key_findings: Dragos tracked 1,266 ransomware incidents affecting industrial organisations in Q3 2026, up 11% from 1,140 in Q2.
Manufacturing accounted for 876 incidents (69%); North America had 566, of which 473 were in the United States.
Qilin claimed 195 victims and The Gentlemen 167; distinct ransomware brands hitting industry rose from 70 to 99.
Entry came through internet-facing edge devices and enterprise applications, often within days of disclosure, and stolen VPN credentials.
Cl0p returned with 35 victims via PTC Windchill and FlexPLM exploitation; no operator was seen manipulating a control system directly.
recommendations: Rotate administrator and VPN credentials, especially on FortiGate appliances.
Enforce MFA on all remote access.
Audit for administrator accounts you did not create.
Patch edge devices and enterprise applications rapidly and run continuous external attack surface management.
Enforce strict policies for remote monitoring and management tools.

Review internet-facing applications, identities, privileged and service accounts and external connections, and check logs for reconnaissance, credential use, admin activity and outbound data transfers.
Report incidents to CERT-In within six hours and unauthorised financial transactions at cybercrime.gov.in or helpline 1930.

One, for CVE-2026-73571 (SaveDraftRequest), lets an ordinary authenticated user send mail as another local mailbox; Rapid7 tested it on Zimbra 10.1.16. The other, for CVE-2026-93637, bypasses the GraphQL authentication rate limit and was validated on 10.1.16 Network Edition. The post gives no fixed versions.
written.plain: Rapid7 published ready-made Metasploit test modules for two Zimbra mail-server flaws, one letting a logged-in user send mail as someone else.
written.exec: Public Metasploit modules now exist for two Zimbra flaws, which makes testing and misuse easier.

written.title: Synology patches critical DSM OAuth flaw (CVSS 9.8) and NGINX HTTP/2 flaw (CVSS 8.1)
written.date_note: Date the Synology advisories SA_26_21 and SA_26_20 were published.
written.summary: Synology published two advisories on 19 November. CVE-2026-120382 (CVSS 9.8) lets a remote attacker without an account read or write arbitrary files or cause denial of service through the DSM OAuth API. CVE-2026-123007 (CVSS 8.1) is an NGINX HTTP/2 heap overflow. Fixes for DSM 7.3 and 7.4 are due by 20 November; the advisories do not mention exploitation.
written.plain: Synology has warned of two serious flaws in the software of its NAS storage devices. Fixed versions are due by 20 November; until then the vendor gives workarounds.
written.exec: NAS devices often hold backups and shared files; an unauthenticated flaw in them is a data-loss and ransomware risk if exposed to the internet.
written.action: Install DSM 7.4.1-90080-2 or 7.3.2-86009-6 when released; meanwhile deactivate the OAuth Service package and disable HTTP/2 in Control Panel, and keep NAS devices off the internet.
written.impact: DSM 7.1 to 7.4 and BeeStation OS 1.5 are listed as affected; DSM 7.2.x, 7.1 and BeeStation OS had no fix yet when read (advisories marked Ongoing).

validation.note: Vendor advisories read in full; GBHackers independently reports the same CVEs and scores. No exploitation stated by either.

written.title: D-Link DIR-600L end-of-life router has critical unauthenticated stack overflow with public proof of concept
written.date_note: INCIBE-CERT advisory INCIBE-2026-896 published November 16.
written.place: Madrid, Spain (INCIBE-CERT, publisher of the advisory)
written.geo_basis: advisory publisher; the flaw affects devices worldwide
written.summary: INCIBE-CERT rates CVE-2026-129354 critical (importance 5). In the D-Link DIR-600L router, hardware revision B, firmware 2.17b02, the hnap_main function does not check the length of the HTTP SOAPAction header, so a remote unauthenticated attacker can overflow a stack buffer. A published proof of concept crashes the CGI process in an emulated setup. INCIBE lists exploitation as not observed. D-Link says revision B is end of life.
written.plain: An old D-Link router that no longer gets updates has a serious flaw that lets anyone on the internet crash it, and a public demonstration exists.
written.exec: Unsupported edge routers cannot be patched and are easy targets once a public proof of concept exists.
written.action: Replace DIR-600L rev B routers with a supported model; until then disable remote administration and limit the management interface to a trusted network.
written.impact: Remote buffer overflow without authentication on an unsupported router; no fix will be issued.

written.summary: The Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-99312 on 18 November: when INIT is emulated with nested SVM active on AMD, KVM can run with a stale MMU context. written.action: Update to a fixed kernel (7.3.5, 6.18.64 or 6.12.118), or as DigitalOcean advises set the kvm_amd nested parameter to 0 until you can.
